title: 24 Modules, Zero Mentions of AI Literacy: Inside Google's AI Educator Series
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Nick Potkalitsky conducts a comprehensive review of Google's AI Educator Series—a free, 24-module professional development program teaching educators to use Gemini in K-16 classrooms. He praises the series for its genuine pedagogical scaffolding, its developmental arc from K-2 through higher education, and its consistent positioning of AI as a tool that amplifies teacher expertise rather than replacing it. However, he identifies a critical gap: the entire program teaches educators how to use AI to build materials for students, but never teaches educators how to teach AI literacy to students themselves. None of the 24 modules ask what new objectives AI itself necessitates, and none operationalize the 'Profile of an AI Ready Graduate' that Google advertises. The article also notes uneven treatment of data security, signs of rapid production (copy-pasted introductions, mismatched module references), and a prompting framework (P.A.R.T.S.) that is introduced well but not connected to questions of student capability development. Potkalitsky concludes that the series is a genuine contribution to practical instructional design but leaves the central question of the era unanswered: how do we move from using AI to build materials for students to using AI to build capacity in students?
points: Google made a strategic pivot from LearnLM (AI trained on pedagogy) to Gemini (general-purpose AI), which shifts the burden of pedagogical reasoning entirely onto teachers expressed through prompts—a reasonable decision, but one that has implications for what teachers need to know.

The P.A.R.T.S. prompting framework (Persona, Aim, Recipients, Theme, Structure) is a scaffolded approach that grows in sophistication across modules, moving from a mnemonic in introductory sessions to something approaching a design methodology in higher education modules.

The most significant gap in the series is that it never teaches AI literacy to students: every module positions the teacher as the Gemini user and the student as recipient of AI-generated materials, missing entirely the question of what students need to know about AI itself.

Educators looking for AI-resistant assessment design should study the higher education architecture module, which requires axonometric drawings and physical models—tasks where expert modification of AI output IS the learning, making pure AI generation insufficient.

Data governance receives inconsistent treatment: the administrator-facing benchmark data module is appropriately specific about privacy protections, but the vibe coding module that teaches teachers to build student-facing apps never addresses what happens to student data in those apps.
quotes: Google moved from building AI that understands pedagogy to training pedagogues to use general-purpose AI. Whether that represents a strategic pivot or a pragmatic concession to what's actually ready for classrooms, the result is the same: the burden of pedagogical reasoning now sits with the teacher, expressed through prompts.

The series also makes a clear and defensible choice to position AI behind the teacher's desk. Every module frames the teacher as the Gemini user and the student as the recipient of Gemini-generated materials. The underlying logic is sound: unscaffolded AI use harms student learning.

The series never teaches educators how to teach AI literacy to students. The modules are entirely organized around pre-existing course objectives: literacy, numeracy, source evaluation, critical thinking. These are the right objectives. But the series never asks what new objectives AI itself necessitates.
Every catalog page displays a banner linking to the 'Profile of an AI Ready Graduate,' but the modules never operationalize it.

The question the series leaves unanswered is the one I keep returning to in my own work: how do we move from using AI to build materials for students toward using AI to build capacity in students? The Google AI Educator Series is a thorough answer to the first question. The second question is still waiting.
Google built a free, structured, badge-bearing training program that takes instructional design seriously across grade bands and roles. It grounds its approach in recognizable pedagogical principles.
